title: Interpenetration
hook: Huayan: each thing contains all things, without blocking each other

segments.voice: Yesterday, Huayan, the school named for a sutra. Your line was the flower garland. Which group of yours looked like flowers on one thread? Today, the idea at that school's heart. Day one thousand three hundred thirty-six.

A lamp is already burning in the corner of the room. Someone comes in and lights a second one on the other side. The room gets brighter. But notice what doesn't happen. The second light doesn't shove the first one out of the way. There's no line down the middle where one lamp's light stops and the other's starts. Both lights fill the whole room, all of it, at the same time, and each is still its own flame. Hold that room in mind. A school of Buddhist teachers in China said the whole world is built a little like it. Their word for it is interpenetration.
screen: `A SECOND LAMP IS LIT.` → `NEITHER LIGHT SHOVES THE OTHER.` → `BOTH FILL THE WHOLE ROOM.`

segments.voice: First, the claim. Huayan teaches that each thing contains all things, and is contained in all things, and that they don't get in each other's way. The school's word for that last part is wu'ai: without obstruction. Second, a step at a time. Huayan teachers spoke of the deep nature of things, which they called principle, and of particular things, which they called events. A cup is an event. Its emptiness, the way it depends on everything else, is principle. Between principle and event, they said, there is no obstruction: the cup's emptiness isn't hiding behind the cup. It's right there in it. Third, the bold step. Then Huayan goes further. Between one event and another event there's no obstruction either. Not just the cup and its nature, but the cup and the table, the cup and the potter, the cup and the person drinking. Each one holds the others, the way each lamp's light holds the room and the other light too. That is interpenetration. Fourth, why that's not the same as everything blurring into one. The second lamp is still the second lamp. You could blow it out, and the first would keep shining. Huayan insists on both halves: each thing is fully itself, in its own place, and each thing holds the whole. That's what without obstruction means. Not a soup where everything melts. A room full of distinct lights, none of them crowding the others out. On an ordinary day, it's a hard and generous way to look at people. Each person whole in their own right, and each one carrying everybody else.
screen: `EACH CONTAINS ALL, WITHOUT BLOCKING.` · `PRINCIPLE AND EVENT, NOT IN THE WAY.` · `EVENT AND EVENT, NOT IN THE WAY.` · `DISTINCT, NOT A SOUP.` · then, large: `WITHOUT OBSTRUCTION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice two things touching. Sit, and let the breath settle. Then find a place where two things meet. Your hand resting on your knee. Your feet on the floor. Your back against the chair. Stay with one meeting. Is the hand touching the knee, or the knee touching the hand? Notice that both are happening, and neither pushes the other out. Each stays itself. Each is changed by the other. When the mind wanders, come back to that one place of touch. The bell holds the time.
Interpenetration. Huayan's teaching that each thing holds all things and is held by them, with nothing blocking anything else. Today's word.
Your line: without obstruction. Today, when someone else's presence feels like it's crowding yours, try picturing two lamps in one room. Day one thousand three hundred thirty-six.

howItsDone: Huayan Buddhists contemplate the interpenetration of principle and event, and of each event with every other, drawing on the Flower Garland Sutra and the commentaries of masters such as Fazang and Chengguan.

fork.setup: you light a second lamp in a room already lit. Huayan asks: what happens to the first lamp's light?
options: it gets pushed into one corner.
it vanishes into the new light.
both fill the whole room, each still itself.
fork.reveal: neither crowds the other out. that picture of distinct things not blocking each other is what Huayan calls without obstruction.

original.note: Chinese shishi wu'ai: event and event without obstruction, Huayan's boldest step.

trapdoor: what you thought: interpenetration means everything is connected.
what it means: each thing contains all things and is contained by them, without any of them blocking the others.
what a scholar hears: principle and event without obstruction, then event and event without obstruction, and each thing still fully distinct.

sources.ref: principle (li) and event (shi); non-obstruction (wu'ai) between principle and event and between event and event
the vision of all things contained in each

notes: Editor pass: hook no longer implies Huayan sources used the two-lamps image (it is the writer's illustration); varied the hook's closing formula.

The scheme of principle/event and the two kinds of non-obstruction is drawn from Chengguan's systematization of the realms of reality (dharmadhatu); counts of realms are deliberately left out. Confirm the simplification.
The two-lamps image is the writer's illustration; Huayan sources use similar images of many lights in one room, but no traditional source is claimed.
Original: 事事無礙, pronunciation shr-shr woo-EYE; confirm.
